rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: The graph of \(y = p(x)\) is given, for a polynomial \(p(x)\). The number of zeroes of \(p(x)\) from the graph is
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the graph of y = p(x) is the whole question: a downward-opening curve drawn on the x and y axes near the origin. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The zeroes of \(p(x)\) are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis. The curve rises from below, just touches the x-axis at one point and turns down again, so it meets the axis exactly once.

The number of zeroes is 1, which is option (B) \(1\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem: The value of k for which the pair of equations \(kx = y + 2\) and \(6x = 2y + 3\) has infinitely many solutions,
rows.solution:
Write the equations as \(kx - y - 2 = 0\) and \(6x - 2y - 3 = 0\). Infinitely many solutions need \(\dfrac{k}{6} = \dfrac{-1}{-2} = \dfrac{-2}{-3}\).

But \(\dfrac{-1}{-2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{-2}{-3} = \dfrac{2}{3}\) are not equal, so no value of k can make all three ratios equal. (With \(k = 3\) the first two ratios agree, but the lines are then parallel and have no solution.)

This is option (B) does not exist.

rows.stem: If \(p - 1\), \(p + 1\) and \(2p + 3\) are in A.P., then the value of p is
rows.solution:
Three numbers are in A.P. when twice the middle one equals the sum of the other two: \(2(p + 1) = (p - 1) + (2p + 3)\).

\(2p + 2 = 3p + 2\), so \(p = 0\), which is option (C) \(0\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: In what ratio, does x-axis divide the line segment joining the points \(A(3, 6)\) and \(B(-12, -3)\) ?
rows.solution:
Let the x-axis divide AB in the ratio \(k : 1\) at a point \((x, 0)\). The y-coordinate of that point is

\(\dfrac{k(-3) + 1(6)}{k + 1} = 0\), so \(-3k + 6 = 0\) and \(k = 2\).

The ratio is \(2 : 1\), which is option (D) \(2 : 1\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, PQ is tangent to the circle centred at O. If \(\angle AOB = 95^\circ\), then the measure of \(\angle ABQ\) will be
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A and B lie on the circle, that the tangent PQ touches it at B, and on which side of B the point Q lies are shown only in the drawing. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
\(OA = OB\) (radii), so in triangle AOB, \(\angle OBA = \angle OAB = \dfrac{180^\circ - 95^\circ}{2} = 42.5^\circ\).

The radius OB is perpendicular to the tangent PQ, so \(\angle OBQ = 90^\circ\), and \(\angle ABQ = 90^\circ - 42.5^\circ = 47.5^\circ\).

This is option (A) \(47.5^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
rows.stem: If \(2\tan A = 3\), then the value of \(\dfrac{4\sin A + 3\cos A}{4\sin A - 3\cos A}\) is
rows.solution:
\(\tan A = \dfrac{3}{2}\). Divide the numerator and denominator by \(\cos A\):

\(\dfrac{4\tan A + 3}{4\tan A - 3} = \dfrac{6 + 3}{6 - 3} = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3\), which is option (C) \(3\).

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: If \(\alpha, \beta\) are the zeroes of a polynomial \(p(x) = x^2 + x - 1\), then \(\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta}\) equals to
rows.solution:
For \(x^2 + x - 1\): \(\alpha + \beta = -1\) and \(\alpha\beta = -1\).

\(\dfrac{1}{\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\beta} = \dfrac{\alpha + \beta}{\alpha\beta} = \dfrac{-1}{-1} = 1\), which is option (A) \(1\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: The least positive value of k, for which the quadratic equation \(2x^2 + kx - 4 = 0\) has rational roots, is
rows.solution:
The roots are rational when the discriminant \(k^2 - 4(2)(-4) = k^2 + 32\) is a perfect square.

Trying positive whole numbers: \(k = 1\) gives 33, not a square; \(k = 2\) gives \(36 = 6^2\). So the least positive value is \(k = 2\), and the equation \(2x^2 + 2x - 4 = 0\) then has the rational roots 1 and \(-2\).

This is option (B) \(2\).

rows.stem: \(\left[\dfrac{3}{4}\tan^2 30^\circ - \sec^2 45^\circ + \sin^2 60^\circ\right]\) is equal to
rows.solution:
\(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), \(\sec 45^\circ = \sqrt{2}\), \(\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{3} - 2 + \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4} - 2 + \dfrac{3}{4} = -1\), which is option (A) \(-1\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Curved surface area of a cylinder of height 5 cm is \(94.2\,\text{cm}^2\). Radius of the cylinder is (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))
rows.solution:
Curved surface area \(= 2\pi r h\), so \(2 \times 3.14 \times r \times 5 = 94.2\).

\(31.4\,r = 94.2\) gives \(r = 3\) cm, which is option (B) 3 cm.

rows.stem:
The distribution below gives the marks obtained by 80 students on a test :

| Marks | Less than 10 | Less than 20 | Less than 30 | Less than 40 | Less than 50 | Less than 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of Students | 3 | 12 | 27 | 57 | 75 | 80 |

The modal class of this distribution is :
rows.solution:
Turn the cumulative frequencies into class frequencies by subtracting each from the next:

0-10: 3, 10-20: \(12 - 3 = 9\), 20-30: \(27 - 12 = 15\), 30-40: \(57 - 27 = 30\), 40-50: \(75 - 57 = 18\), 50-60: \(80 - 75 = 5\).

The highest frequency is 30, so the modal class is 30-40, which is option (C) \(30 - 40\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: The curved surface area of a cone having height 24 cm and radius 7 cm, is
rows.solution:
Slant height \(l = \sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25\) cm.

Curved surface area \(= \pi r l = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550\,\text{cm}^2\), which is option (C) \(550\,\text{cm}^2\).

rows.stem: The distance between the points \((0, 2\sqrt{5})\) and \((-2\sqrt{5}, 0)\) is
rows.solution:
Distance \(= \sqrt{(-2\sqrt{5} - 0)^2 + (0 - 2\sqrt{5})^2} = \sqrt{20 + 20} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\) units.

This is option (A) \(2\sqrt{10}\) units.

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: Which of the following is a quadratic polynomial having zeroes \(\dfrac{-2}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) ?
rows.solution:
A quadratic with zeroes \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) is a multiple of \(\left(x + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)\left(x - \dfrac{2}{3}\right) = x^2 - \dfrac{4}{9}\), that is of \(9x^2 - 4\).

\(5(9x^2 - 4)\) is such a multiple. (The polynomial \(4x^2 - 9\) has zeroes \(\pm\dfrac{3}{2}\), and the other two have no real zeroes.)

This is option (D) \(5(9x^2 - 4)\).

rows.stem: If the value of each observation of a statistical data is increased by 3, then the mean of the data
rows.solution:
If the observations are \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) with mean \(\bar{x}\), the new mean is

\(\dfrac{(x_1 + 3) + (x_2 + 3) + \cdots + (x_n + 3)}{n} = \dfrac{\sum x_i + 3n}{n} = \bar{x} + 3\).

The mean increases by 3, which is option (B) increases by 3.

rows.stem: Probability of happening of an event is denoted by p and probability of non-happening of the event is denoted by q. Relation between p and q is
rows.solution:
The event either happens or does not happen, so the two probabilities add up to 1: \(p + q = 1\).

This is option (A) \(p + q = 1\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: A girl calculates that the probability of her winning the first prize in a lottery is 0.08. If 6000 tickets are sold, how many tickets has she bought ?
rows.solution:
\(P(\text{winning}) = \dfrac{\text{tickets she bought}}{6000} = 0.08\), so she bought \(0.08 \times 6000 = 480\) tickets.

This is option (C) \(480\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: In a group of 20 people, 5 can't swim. If one person is selected at random, then the probability that he/she can swim, is
rows.solution:
\(20 - 5 = 15\) people can swim.

\(P(\text{can swim}) = \dfrac{15}{20} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), which is option (A) \(\dfrac{3}{4}\).

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** Point \(P(0, 2)\) is the point of intersection of y-axis with the line \(3x + 2y = 4\).

**Reason (R) :** The distance of point \(P(0, 2)\) from x-axis is 2 units.
rows.context: In Question 19 and 20, an **Assertion (A)** statement is followed by a statement of **Reason (R)**. Select the correct option out of the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
On the y-axis \(x = 0\), so \(3(0) + 2y = 4\) gives \(y = 2\). The line meets the y-axis at \(P(0, 2)\), and the Assertion is true.

The distance of a point from the x-axis is the absolute value of its y-coordinate, here 2 units, so the Reason is true. But this distance says nothing about where the line meets the y-axis, so the Reason does not explain the Assertion.

Both statements are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The perimeter of \(\Delta ABC\) is a rational number.

**Reason (R) :** The sum of the squares of two rational numbers is always rational.
rows.context: In Question 19 and 20, an **Assertion (A)** statement is followed by a statement of **Reason (R)**. Select the correct option out of the following :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the triangle's measurements (the two sides about B and the right angle at B) are given only in the drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
In the figure \(AB = 2\) cm, \(BC = 3\) cm and \(\angle B = 90^\circ\). By Pythagoras, \(AC = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{13}\) cm.

Perimeter \(= 2 + 3 + \sqrt{13} = (5 + \sqrt{13})\) cm. \(\sqrt{13}\) is irrational, so the perimeter is irrational, and the Assertion is false.

If a and b are rational, \(a^2\) and \(b^2\) are rational, and so is their sum. The Reason is true.

The Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: Solve the pair of equations \(x = 3\) and \(y = -4\) graphically.
rows.solution:
Draw both lines on the same axes.

\(x = 3\) is the vertical line through \((3, 0)\), parallel to the y-axis.

\(y = -4\) is the horizontal line through \((0, -4)\), parallel to the x-axis.

The two lines meet at the point \((3, -4)\). So the solution is \(x = 3\), \(y = -4\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem:
Using graphical method, find whether following system of linear equations is consistent or not :

\(x = 0\) and \(y = -7\)
rows.solution:
\(x = 0\) is the y-axis itself, and \(y = -7\) is the horizontal line through \((0, -7)\), parallel to the x-axis.

Drawn on the same axes, the line \(y = -7\) cuts the y-axis at \((0, -7)\). The lines meet in exactly one point, so the system is consistent, with the unique solution \(x = 0\), \(y = -7\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, XZ is parallel to BC. AZ = 3 cm, ZC = 2 cm, BM = 3 cm and MC = 5 cm. Find the length of XY.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the points M on BC and Y on XZ (where AM crosses XZ), and X on AB and Z on AC, are defined only in the drawing. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
\(XZ \parallel BC\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AX}{XB} = \dfrac{AZ}{ZC} = \dfrac{3}{2}\). So \(\dfrac{AX}{AB} = \dfrac{3}{3 + 2} = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

In triangles AXY and ABM: \(\angle AXY = \angle ABM\) (corresponding angles, since \(XY \parallel BM\)) and \(\angle A\) is common. So \(\Delta AXY \sim \Delta ABM\) (AA similarity).

\(\dfrac{XY}{BM} = \dfrac{AX}{AB} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(XY = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 3 = \dfrac{9}{5} = 1.8\) cm.

rows.stem: If \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\), then find the value of \(\sin\theta \cdot \cos\theta\).
rows.solution:
Squaring both sides of \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\):

\(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 3\)

\(1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = 3\), so \(\sin\theta \cdot \cos\theta = 1\).

Note that no real angle satisfies the given condition, since \(\sin\theta + \cos\theta \le \sqrt{2}\) for every angle.

rows.stem: If \(\sin\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\cot\beta = \sqrt{3}\), then find the value of \(\operatorname{cosec}\alpha + \operatorname{cosec}\beta\).
rows.solution:
\(\sin\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\operatorname{cosec}\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sin\alpha} = \sqrt{2}\).

\(\operatorname{cosec}\beta = \sqrt{1 + \cot^2\beta} = \sqrt{1 + 3} = 2\).

\(\operatorname{cosec}\alpha + \operatorname{cosec}\beta = \sqrt{2} + 2\), or \(\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2} + 1)\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: Find the greatest number which divides 85 and 72 leaving remainders 1 and 2 respectively.
rows.solution:
A number that leaves remainder 1 on 85 and remainder 2 on 72 divides \(85 - 1 = 84\) and \(72 - 2 = 70\) exactly. The greatest such number is the HCF of 84 and 70.

\(84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7\) and \(70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7\), so HCF \(= 2 \times 7 = 14\).

The required number is 14. (Check: \(85 = 6 \times 14 + 1\) and \(72 = 5 \times 14 + 2\).)

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 yellow balls. One ball is drawn at random from the bag. Find the probability that drawn ball is (i) red (ii) yellow.
rows.solution:
The bag has \(4 + 3 + 2 = 9\) balls.

(i) \(P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{4}{9}\).

(ii) \(P(\text{yellow}) = \dfrac{2}{9}\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.stem: Half of the difference between two numbers is 2. The sum of the greater number and twice the smaller number is 13. Find the numbers.
rows.solution:
Let the numbers be x and y, with \(x > y\).

Half the difference is 2: \(\dfrac{1}{2}(x - y) = 2\), that is \(x - y = 4\) ... (i)

The greater plus twice the smaller is 13: \(x + 2y = 13\) ... (ii)

From (i), \(x = y + 4\). Substituting in (ii): \(y + 4 + 2y = 13\), so \(3y = 9\) and \(y = 3\); then \(x = 7\).

The numbers are 7 and 3.

rows.stem: If \((-5, 3)\) and \((5, 3)\) are two vertices of an equilateral triangle, then find coordinates of the third vertex, given that origin lies inside the triangle. (Take \(\sqrt{3} = 1.7\))
rows.solution:
Let the vertices be \(A(-5, 3)\), \(B(5, 3)\) and \(C(x, y)\). Then \(AB = 10\).

In an equilateral triangle \(CA = CB\): \((x + 5)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = (x - 5)^2 + (y - 3)^2\), which gives \(20x = 0\), so \(x = 0\).

Also \(CA = AB = 10\): \((0 + 5)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = 100\), so \((y - 3)^2 = 75\) and \(y - 3 = \pm 5\sqrt{3}\).

The side AB lies on the line \(y = 3\), above the origin. For the origin to lie inside the triangle, C must be below the x-axis, so \(y = 3 - 5\sqrt{3} = 3 - 5 \times 1.7 = -5.5\).

The third vertex is \((0, -5.5)\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that \(\angle PTQ = 2\angle OPQ\).
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the circle with centre O, the tangents TP and TQ, the chord PQ and the radius OP; the stem states the configuration in full. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Let \(\angle PTQ = \theta\).

Tangents from an external point are equal, so \(TP = TQ\) and triangle TPQ is isosceles: \(\angle TPQ = \angle TQP = \dfrac{180^\circ - \theta}{2} = 90^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

The radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP, so \(\angle OPT = 90^\circ\).

\(\angle OPQ = \angle OPT - \angle TPQ = 90^\circ - \left(90^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\theta}{2}\).

So \(\angle PTQ = \theta = 2\angle OPQ\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: In the given figure, a circle is inscribed in a quadrilateral ABCD in which \(\angle B = 90^\circ\). If AD = 17 cm, AB = 20 cm and DS = 3 cm, then find the radius of the circle.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the points of contact are named only in the drawing: R on AD, S on DC, P on BC and Q on AB, with radii OP and OQ marked r. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Tangents from an external point are equal.

From D: \(DR = DS = 3\) cm, so \(AR = AD - DR = 17 - 3 = 14\) cm.

From A: \(AQ = AR = 14\) cm, so \(QB = AB - AQ = 20 - 14 = 6\) cm.

\(OQ \perp AB\), \(OP \perp BC\) and \(\angle B = 90^\circ\), with \(OQ = OP = r\). So OQBP is a square, and \(r = OP = QB = 6\) cm.

The radius of the circle is 6 cm.

rows.stem: Prove that : \(\dfrac{\tan\theta + \sec\theta - 1}{\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1} = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\)
rows.solution:
Replace the 1 in the numerator by \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta\):

LHS \(= \dfrac{(\tan\theta + \sec\theta) - (\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta)}{\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\tan\theta + \sec\theta) - (\sec\theta - \tan\theta)(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)}{\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\tan\theta + \sec\theta)(1 - \sec\theta + \tan\theta)}{\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1} = \tan\theta + \sec\theta\)

\(= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A room is in the form of cylinder surmounted by a hemi-spherical dome. The base radius of hemisphere is one-half the height of cylindrical part. Find total height of the room if it contains \(\left(\dfrac{1408}{21}\right)\,\text{m}^3\) of air. \(\left(\text{Take } \pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
rows.solution:
Let r m be the radius of the hemisphere and h m the height of the cylinder, so \(h = 2r\).

Volume of the room \(= \pi r^2 h + \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = 2\pi r^3 + \dfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{8}{3}\pi r^3\).

\(\dfrac{8}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r^3 = \dfrac{1408}{21}\), that is \(\dfrac{176}{21} r^3 = \dfrac{1408}{21}\), so \(r^3 = 8\) and \(r = 2\).

Then \(h = 4\), and the total height of the room is \(h + r = 4 + 2 = 6\) m.

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: An empty cone is of radius 3 cm and height 12 cm. Ice-cream is filled in it so that lower part of the cone which is \(\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)^{\text{th}}\) of the volume of the cone is unfilled but hemisphere is formed on the top. Find volume of the ice-cream. (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - an inverted cone with a hemisphere on its open top; every value is in the stem. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Volume of the cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 3^2 \times 12 = 36\pi\ \text{cm}^3\).

One sixth of the cone is unfilled, so the ice-cream inside the cone is \(\dfrac{5}{6} \times 36\pi = 30\pi\ \text{cm}^3\).

The hemisphere on top has radius 3 cm: its volume is \(\dfrac{2}{3}\pi \times 3^3 = 18\pi\ \text{cm}^3\).

Volume of the ice-cream \(= 30\pi + 18\pi = 48\pi = 48 \times 3.14 = 150.72\ \text{cm}^3\).

rows.stem: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides at distinct points, prove that the other two sides are divided in the same ratio.
rows.solution:
Given: in triangle ABC, a line parallel to BC meets AB at D and AC at E. To prove: \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Construction: join BE and CD, and draw \(DM \perp AC\) and \(EN \perp AB\).

Proof: \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(BDE)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AD \cdot EN}{\frac{1}{2} DB \cdot EN} = \dfrac{AD}{DB}\), and \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(ADE)}{\text{ar}(DEC)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} AE \cdot DM}{\frac{1}{2} EC \cdot DM} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

Triangles BDE and DEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC, so \(\text{ar}(BDE) = \text{ar}(DEC)\). Hence \(\dfrac{AD}{DB} = \dfrac{AE}{EC}\).

rows.stem: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower 24 m high from the foot of another tower in the same plane is \(60^\circ\). The angle of elevation of the top of second tower from the foot of the first tower is \(30^\circ\). Find the distance between two towers and the height of the other tower. Also, find the length of the wire attached to the tops of both the towers.
rows.solution:
Let AB be the 24 m tower (A its foot, B its top) and CD the other tower of height h m (C its foot, D its top), with \(AC = x\) m.

From C, the angle of elevation of B is \(60^\circ\): \(\tan 60^\circ = \dfrac{24}{x} = \sqrt{3}\), so \(x = \dfrac{24}{\sqrt{3}} = 8\sqrt{3}\) ... (i)

From A, the angle of elevation of D is \(30^\circ\): \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(x = h\sqrt{3}\) ... (ii)

From (i) and (ii), \(h\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3}\), so \(h = 8\).

The towers are \(8\sqrt{3}\) m apart, and the other tower is 8 m high.

For the wire BD, draw DE perpendicular to AB. Then \(ED = x = 8\sqrt{3}\) m and \(BE = 24 - 8 = 16\) m, so

\(BD = \sqrt{BE^2 + ED^2} = \sqrt{256 + 192} = \sqrt{448} = 8\sqrt{7}\) m.

The wire is \(8\sqrt{7}\) m long.

rows.stem: A spherical balloon of radius r subtends an angle of \(60^\circ\) at the eye of an observer. If the angle of elevation of its centre is \(45^\circ\) from the same point, then prove that height of the centre of the balloon is \(\sqrt{2}\) times its radius.
rows.solution:
Let B be the observer's eye, O the centre of the balloon and BQ, BP the tangents from B to the balloon, with OA the perpendicular from O to the ground through B.

The balloon subtends \(\angle QBP = 60^\circ\), and BO bisects the angle between the two tangents, so \(\angle PBO = 30^\circ\). The angle of elevation of the centre is \(\angle ABO = 45^\circ\).

The radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent BP, so in right triangle BPO: \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{OP}{OB} = \dfrac{r}{OB}\), so \(OB = 2r\) ... (i)

In right triangle BAO: \(\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{OA}{OB}\), so \(OA = \dfrac{OB}{\sqrt{2}}\) ... (ii)

From (i) and (ii), \(OA = \dfrac{2r}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}\,r\).

So the height of the centre of the balloon is \(\sqrt{2}\) times its radius.

rows.stem: A chord of a circle of radius 14 cm subtends an angle of \(60^\circ\) at the centre. Find the area of the corresponding minor segment of the circle. Also find the area of the major segment of the circle.
rows.solution:
The chord and the two radii form an equilateral triangle of side 14 cm, since the angle at the centre is \(60^\circ\).

Area of the sector \(= \dfrac{60}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14 = \dfrac{308}{3}\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the triangle \(= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 14 \times \sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 14 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 49\sqrt{3}\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the minor segment \(= \left(\dfrac{308}{3} - 49\sqrt{3}\right)\ \text{cm}^2\). Taking \(\sqrt{3} = 1.73\), this is \(102.67 - 84.77 \approx 17.9\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the circle \(= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14 = 616\ \text{cm}^2\).

Area of the major segment \(= 616 - \left(\dfrac{308}{3} - 49\sqrt{3}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1540}{3} + 49\sqrt{3}\right)\ \text{cm}^2 \approx 513.33 + 84.77 \approx 598.1\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The ratio of the \(11^{\text{th}}\) term to \(17^{\text{th}}\) term of an A.P. is 3 : 4. Find the ratio of \(5^{\text{th}}\) term to \(21^{\text{st}}\) term of the same A.P. Also, find the ratio of the sum of first 5 terms to that of first 21 terms.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a and the common difference d.

\(\dfrac{a_{11}}{a_{17}} = \dfrac{a + 10d}{a + 16d} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), so \(4a + 40d = 3a + 48d\) and \(a = 8d\) ... (i)

\(\dfrac{a_5}{a_{21}} = \dfrac{a + 4d}{a + 20d} = \dfrac{8d + 4d}{8d + 20d} = \dfrac{12d}{28d} = \dfrac{3}{7}\), so \(a_5 : a_{21} = 3 : 7\).

\(\dfrac{S_5}{S_{21}} = \dfrac{\frac{5}{2}(2a + 4d)}{\frac{21}{2}(2a + 20d)} = \dfrac{5(16d + 4d)}{21(16d + 20d)} = \dfrac{5 \times 20d}{21 \times 36d} = \dfrac{25}{189}\).

So \(S_5 : S_{21} = 25 : 189\).

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem:
250 logs are stacked in the following manner :

22 logs in the bottom row, 21 in the next row, 20 in the row next to it and so on (as shown by an example). In how many rows, are the 250 logs placed and how many logs are there in the top row ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a small stack of logs captioned '(Example)', four in the bottom row and three above; the stem gives every number. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
Let the number of rows be n. The rows hold 22, 21, 20, 19, ... logs, an AP with \(a = 22\), \(d = -1\), and \(S_n = 250\).

\(250 = \dfrac{n}{2}[2 \times 22 + (n - 1)(-1)] = \dfrac{n}{2}(45 - n)\)

\(500 = 45n - n^2\), so \(n^2 - 45n + 500 = 0\) and \((n - 20)(n - 25) = 0\).

\(n = 25\) would make the top row \(a_{25} = 22 + 24(-1) = -2\), and a row cannot hold a negative number of logs. So \(n = 20\).

Logs in the top row \(= a_{20} = 22 + 19(-1) = 3\).

The 250 logs are placed in 20 rows, with 3 logs in the top row.

rows.stem: Write an algebraic equation depicting the above information.
rows.context:
While designing the school year book, a teacher asked the student that the length and width of a particular photo is increased by \(x\) units each to double the area of the photo. The original photo is 18 cm long and 12 cm wide.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the 18 cm by 12 cm school photo inside the enlarged rectangle, with the increase x marked on the length and the width; every value is in the passage. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The new photo is \((18 + x)\) cm long and \((12 + x)\) cm wide, and its area is double the original:

\((18 + x)(12 + x) = 2(18 \times 12)\).

rows.stem: Write the corresponding quadratic equation in standard form.
rows.context:

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: What should be the new dimensions of the enlarged photo ?
rows.context:
While designing the school year book, a teacher asked the student that the length and width of a particular photo is increased by \(x\) units each to double the area of the photo. The original photo is 18 cm long and 12 cm wide.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
Doubling the area gives \((18 + x)(12 + x) = 2 \times 18 \times 12 = 432\), that is \(x^2 + 30x - 216 = 0\).

\(x^2 + 36x - 6x - 216 = (x + 36)(x - 6) = 0\), so \(x = 6\) or \(x = -36\). The increase cannot be negative, so \(x = 6\).

The enlarged photo is \(18 + 6 = 24\) cm long and \(12 + 6 = 18\) cm wide: 24 cm by 18 cm.

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: Can any rational value of \(x\) make the new area equal to \(220\,\text{cm}^2\) ?
rows.context:
While designing the school year book, a teacher asked the student that the length and width of a particular photo is increased by \(x\) units each to double the area of the photo. The original photo is 18 cm long and 12 cm wide.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.solution:
A new area of \(220\ \text{cm}^2\) needs \((18 + x)(12 + x) = 220\), that is \(x^2 + 30x + 216 = 220\), or \(x^2 + 30x - 4 = 0\).

Discriminant \(D = 30^2 - 4(1)(-4) = 900 + 16 = 916\), which is not a perfect square. So the roots are irrational.

No rational value of x can make the new area \(220\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.stem: find the length of AB.
rows.context:
The discus throw is an event in which an athlete attempts to throw a discus. The athlete spins anti-clockwise around one and a half times through a circle, then releases the throw. When released, the discus travels along tangent to the circular spin orbit.

In the given figure, AB is one such tangent to a circle of radius 75 cm. Point O is centre of the circle and \(\angle ABO = 30^\circ\). PQ is parallel to OA.

Based on above information :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A, the end of the 75 cm radius OA, is the point where AB touches the circle is shown only in the drawing; the discus-thrower photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
AB touches the circle at A, so the radius OA is perpendicular to AB and triangle OAB is right-angled at A.

\(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{OA}{AB}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{75}{AB}\) and \(AB = 75\sqrt{3}\) cm.

rows.stem: find the length of OB.
rows.context:
The discus throw is an event in which an athlete attempts to throw a discus. The athlete spins anti-clockwise around one and a half times through a circle, then releases the throw. When released, the discus travels along tangent to the circular spin orbit.

In the given figure, AB is one such tangent to a circle of radius 75 cm. Point O is centre of the circle and \(\angle ABO = 30^\circ\). PQ is parallel to OA.

Based on above information :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A, the end of the 75 cm radius OA, is the point where AB touches the circle is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent AB, so triangle OAB is right-angled at A.

\(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{OA}{OB}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{75}{OB}\) and \(OB = 150\) cm.

rows.stem: find the length of AP.
rows.context:
The discus throw is an event in which an athlete attempts to throw a discus. The athlete spins anti-clockwise around one and a half times through a circle, then releases the throw. When released, the discus travels along tangent to the circular spin orbit.

In the given figure, AB is one such tangent to a circle of radius 75 cm. Point O is centre of the circle and \(\angle ABO = 30^\circ\). PQ is parallel to OA.

Based on above information :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the passage never places P or Q: only the drawing puts Q on OB where it crosses the circle and P on AB, with A the point of contact. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
In right triangle OAB (right-angled at A, since the radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent AB): \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{75}{OB}\) gives \(OB = 150\) cm, and \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{75}{AB}\) gives \(AB = 75\sqrt{3}\) cm.

Q lies on the circle, so \(OQ = 75\) cm and \(QB = 150 - 75 = 75\) cm. So Q is the mid-point of OB.

In triangle BOA, \(PQ \parallel OA\) and passes through the mid-point Q of OB, so P is the mid-point of AB.

\(AP = \dfrac{AB}{2} = \dfrac{75\sqrt{3}}{2}\) cm.

rows.stem: find the length of PQ.
rows.context:
The discus throw is an event in which an athlete attempts to throw a discus. The athlete spins anti-clockwise around one and a half times through a circle, then releases the throw. When released, the discus travels along tangent to the circular spin orbit.

In the given figure, AB is one such tangent to a circle of radius 75 cm. Point O is centre of the circle and \(\angle ABO = 30^\circ\). PQ is parallel to OA.

Based on above information :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the passage never places P or Q: only the drawing puts Q on OB where it crosses the circle and P on AB, with A the point of contact. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
In right triangle OAB (right-angled at A, since the radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent AB): \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{75}{OB}\) gives \(OB = 150\) cm. Q lies on the circle, so \(OQ = 75\) cm and \(QB = 150 - 75 = 75\) cm.

\(PQ \parallel OA\), so in triangles BQP and BOA, \(\angle BQP = \angle BOA\) (corresponding angles) and \(\angle B\) is common. So \(\Delta BQP \sim \Delta BOA\) (AA similarity).

\(\dfrac{PQ}{OA} = \dfrac{QB}{OB} = \dfrac{75}{150} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(PQ = \dfrac{75}{2} = 37.5\) cm.
